classification.difficultyReason: Identify the correct difference graph and explain the missing reflection in the incorrect construction.

inlines.text: Bob and Mary each attempted to graph
Who is correct? What error has been made in the incorrect answer?

spec.description: Two labelled, unscaled curves on common axes. The blue curve descends to a broad trough and rises; the red curve decreases. They share a positive y-intercept and intersect again below the x-axis.
spec.mathematics: Qualitative unscaled reconstruction. TikZ coordinates are drawing normalisation only, not source numerical givens or asserted function equations. No ticks, grid or origin label are printed.
spec.answerVisibility: Both supplied component graphs and their labels remain visible.

spec.description: Boxed name above a solid orange candidate curve. The candidate starts above the axis, descends through it into a broad trough and returns to the axis at the right. Faint dashed component curves remain visible.
spec.mathematics: Qualitative unscaled reconstruction using the same component-curve drawing frame as the given graph. Candidate ordinates represent the sum of the two original component sketches; this interpretation is not printed in the student diagram.
spec.answerVisibility: This is Bob's supplied attempt, permanently visible as question evidence.

spec.description: Boxed name above a solid orange candidate curve starting at the origin, descending into a trough and rising through the x-axis. Dashed blue and reflected red reference curves remain visible.
spec.mathematics: Qualitative unscaled reconstruction in the same component-curve drawing frame. Candidate ordinates represent f minus g. The dashed red reference is the vertical reflection of the original red sketch; no additional explanatory labels are printed.
spec.answerVisibility: This is Mary's supplied attempt, permanently visible as question evidence.

answer.short: Mary is correct. Bob added $g(x)$ instead of $-g(x)$; he needed to reflect $y=g(x)$ in the $x$-axis first.
answer.worked:
Reflect $y=g(x)$ in the $x$-axis to obtain $y=-g(x)$, then add its ordinates to those of $y=f(x)$ at each $x$.

Mary is correct. Where the original curves intersect, their difference is zero, as shown in her graph.

Bob added the original ordinates, producing $y=f(x)+g(x)$ instead.
